2
What is the ohm expressed in SI base units?
A
kg m2
s–3
A–2
B
kg–1
m–2
s3
A2
C
J C–1
A–1
D
W A–2

hints: Start from the definition of resistance from $R = V/I$, so $1$ ohm is $1$ volt per ampere and has units $\text{V A}^{-1}$.
Recall that volt can be written with joule and coulomb as $V = \text{J C}^{-1}$, where $\text{J} = \text{N m}$ and $\text{C} = \text{A s}$.
Expand $\text{N}$ to $\text{kg m s}^{-2}$ and collect the powers of $\text{kg}$, $\text{m}$, $\text{s}$ and $\text{A}$ to get only base units.
walkthrough: Identify the defining relation: $R = V/I$, so the unit ohm $\Omega$ is $\text{V A}^{-1}$.
Write volt in other derived units: $V = \text{J C}^{-1}$ because potential difference is energy per charge.
Expand joule and coulomb to base-related units: $\text{J} = \text{N m} = (\text{kg m s}^{-2})(\text{m}) = \text{kg m}^2 \text{s}^{-2}$ and $\text{C} = \text{A s}$.
Substitute to get volt in base units: $V = \text{kg m}^2 \text{s}^{-2} / (\text{A s}) = \text{kg m}^2 \text{s}^{-3} \text{A}^{-1}$.
Divide by one more ampere for resistance: $\Omega = V/\text{A} = \text{kg m}^2 \text{s}^{-3} \text{A}^{-2}$.
Options C and D still contain derived units $\text{J}$, $\text{C}$ and $\text{W}$, and option B has all powers inverted. This is option A.

A.explanation: This is $\text{kg m}^2 \text{s}^{-3} \text{A}^{-2}$, which follows from $R = V/I$ expanded fully to base units.

B.explanation: This is the inverse of the ohm, with all powers reversed, and is the unit of conductance in base units.

C.explanation: Since $V = \text{J C}^{-1}$, this equals $\text{V A}^{-1}$, but joule and coulomb are not SI base units.

D.explanation: Since $V = \text{W A}^{-1}$, this equals $\text{V A}^{-1}$, but watt is a derived unit, not a base unit.
